chapter.title: Not Mine to Open
chapter.sub: Know the arithmetic. Know whose door it is.

items.text: SEASON 1 · EPISODE 5 · DRAFT  Countdown · Maya and Malik · Level L2 (Operator)  Sofia adds twelve fixtures for Easter, and a stage circuit trips during rehearsal. Maya can do the arithmetic. Only the electricians may open the panel.

items.title: Not Mine to Open
items.stakes: Half the stage is dead fifteen hours before Easter. The breaker is behind a door that isn't yours.
items.reward: Easter at full brightness — and a call the electrician remembers for the right reasons.

objectives.text: Make it safe before you make it work
Escalate with a load table, not a panic
Do the arithmetic Andre will check
Tell Sofia what full brightness really costs
Look closer: find two things behind the stage

items.rumor: The panel schedule is dated 1998. Circuit 3 is labeled STAGE (TEMP).

items.alt: Sofia unpacks new lighting fixtures on the stage while Theo carries boxes.

bubbles.text: Twelve more for Easter. Where's the nearest outlet?
Four right here, by the drums!

items.alt: In the booth, Maya's radio crackles: Theo, reporting a change before he makes it.

bubbles.text: Heads up — Sofia's plugging in twelve lights by the drums.
Thanks for telling me first. Which outlets are those on?

items.caption: Theo tells her before, not after. (Payoff: S01E00.)

items.alt: Theo looks at the wall outlets by the drums. There's no label on them at all.

bubbles.text: …On the wall?

items.caption: Nobody knows which circuit they're on.

items.alt: Rehearsal. Sofia brings the Easter look up to full: every new fixture blazes. The band plays; Marisol sings.
items.caption: Sofia brings the Easter look to full.

items.alt: Half the stage goes dark. The keyboard and the stage-left monitors go silent too.
items.caption: Half the stage goes dark. The keyboard dies. So do the stage-left monitors.

lines.text: That was twelve lights and a very large THUNK.

items.alt: Pastor Jo, in the half-dark, deadpans.

bubbles.text: Is that the resurrection cue? Because it's early.

lines.text: Is that the resurrection cue? Because it's early.
(Nobody laughs. Then everybody does. Then the stage stays dark.)

items.alt: Imani hurries into the booth. Easter morning is fifteen hours away.

bubbles.text: The breaker's in the electrical room, right? Can we just flip it back on?

items.prompt: Half the stage is dead, fifteen hours before Easter. What do you do first?
items.happening: The stage-left outlets are dead; everything else works.
known: ◉ Twelve new fixtures went in today
◉ It tripped when the look went to full
items.risk: Easter morning, and anyone near a circuit nobody understands.
timeout: Sofia runs a cord across the stage while you decide.
Make safe first — it's the only move that can't make things worse.

hints.text: What changed today, and when exactly did it fail?
A breaker is designed to open when a circuit is asked for too much.
List everything plugged into the dead outlets and read each nameplate.
Power is volts times amps. Add the loads and compare.
Walkthrough, then a variant: a coffee urn and a heater on one fellowship-hall circuit.

items.note: Draft decision (DR-S01E05). Options A and B are shown to be stopped or costly: the story never depicts resetting or re-routing building power as the team's job.

options.label: Reset the breaker
options.result: The electrical room is locked, and it isn't the team's. Imani: “You're right. Not ours.” Back to the choice.
options.consequence: If it tripped for a reason, resetting it just repeats the reason — or hides a worse one.
options.fail: Resetting a breaker you don't own repeats the overload — or worse.

options.label: Run a cord to another outlet
options.result: Sofia likes it. A cord snakes across the stage to the far wall — and nobody knows what that circuit carries either.
options.consequence: It could trip the second circuit too, and the cord is a trip hazard on a dark stage.
options.fail: Moving an unknown load to an unknown circuit spreads the problem.

options.label: Make safe, then list the loads
options.result: Lights to zero at the desk, people clear of stage-left gear, and a list of everything that was plugged in there.
options.consequence: She arrives at the phone call with facts, not a guess.

options.label: Ask Sofia to use fewer lights
options.result: Sofia, hurt: “Which ones? Half of Easter?”
options.consequence: Nobody knows how many is too many, so any number is a guess.

items.title: The breaker isn't broken
items.body: Everyone calls it a faulty breaker. The nameplates add up to about 22.5 A on a 20 A circuit. The breaker did its job perfectly; twelve fixtures were added without asking what the circuit could carry.

items.alt: Maya takes charge calmly: lights to zero, people clear.

bubbles.text: Sofia, take the lights to zero at the desk. Everyone off the stage-left gear. Nobody plugs anything anywhere.

items.alt: Maya walks the paths. System View: the stage-left power lane is dark; the booth and the other stage outlets are fine. The lighting console still works; the keyboard is dead only because its power is.
narration: Power: only stage left. Control: the lighting desk still answers. Signal: the keyboard is dead only because its power is.

items.alt: Close-up: the nameplate sticker on the back of a new fixture reads 150 W, 120 V — an example rating. Maya copies it without opening anything.
items.caption: She reads the label on the outside. She doesn't open anything.

items.title: A second label, under the first
items.body: The new sign says ELECTRICAL — AUTHORIZED ONLY. Under it, peeling: *R. has key.* Ray gave the key back years ago. The sign didn't get the message.

items.alt: Maya's load table: 12 new fixtures, 1,800 watts; keyboard and amp, 400; two monitors, 400; pedalboard and miscellaneous, 100; total 2,700 watts. All example numbers from nameplates.
items.caption: Nameplate numbers (example). What was on the stage-left outlets when it tripped.

items.text: 🔭 PHYSICS IN MOTION  Current, heat and a 20 A breaker  The science under this episode’s problem — live.

items.sub: Beginner · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Ray and Maya beside a board. Current is watts divided by volts. A twelve-hundred-watt heater on a hundred-twenty volts draws ten amps. And the breaker? Plan to eighty percent: a fifteen-amp breaker gives a twelve-amp planning line. The panel is the electrician's. That's a boundary — we bring the numbers, not a screwdriver.

bubbles.text: Current is watts divided by volts. A twelve-hundred-watt heater on a hundred-twenty volts draws ten amps.
And the breaker?
Plan to eighty percent: a fifteen-amp breaker gives a twelve-amp planning line. The panel is the electrician's. That's a boundary — we bring the numbers, not a screwdriver.

items.caption: Beginner: the term, what it means, the formula — and one worked example out loud.

items.text: 📘 RAY'S NOTEBOOK · BEGINNER  Terms    Current   Flow of electricity, in amperes (A).   Breaker   A switch that trips when current is too high, protecting the wiring. Resetting it is the electrician's call.   Boundary   A line you don't cross because a system or decision belongs to someone else — power, rigging, towers, security, evacuations.   Formula, variables and a worked example   ƒ FORMULA · Current from power  I = P ÷ V   I  current, A  P  power, W  V  voltage, V    Worked example.  A 1,200 W heater on 120 V: 1,200 ÷ 120 = 10 A.    ƒ FORMULA · Continuous-load planning line  I plan  = 0.8 × I breaker    I breaker   breaker rating, A  0.8  80% planning line (illustrative; local code rules)    Worked example.  A 15 A breaker: 0.8 × 15 = 12 A planning line.

📒 EMPATHIA LEARN FIELDBOOK · MODULE 06 OF 31 · PP. 9, 110, 114  PART 1 CORE TECHNOLOGY FOUNDATIONS · PART 7 RF, LOW VOLTAGE & ELECTRICAL  Page 110. Ray had boxed one sentence —  the electrician owns the panel  — and written underneath: “Your math starts the conversation. It doesn't open the door.”

items.label: **Fieldbook module 6 — Electricity basics — and whose panel it is.** Beginner support: every new word is defined, and every formula comes with its variables and a worked example.

items.text: 📖 From the Fieldbook · module 6 · tap a plate to open it full size     AV math and physics basics     Power, grounding and electrical safety     Low-voltage electrical engineering and safety basics

items.alt: The booth whiteboard: P equals V times I. One example 20-amp circuit at 120 volts: 2,400 watts. They asked for 2,700 watts, which is 22.5 amps. The breaker did its job. Illustrative; the electrician has the real numbers.
Maya explains to Imani why they won't flip the breaker themselves.

bubbles.text: It tripped because we asked too much of it. If we reset it and I'm wrong about why, we find out the hard way.
And it's not our room.

items.prompt: It's a switch, Maya. My dad reset breakers for forty years. Why are we standing here?

options.label: “Because if I'm wrong about why it tripped, we find out the hard way — and it's not our room.”
options.reply: …Okay. I hate that you're right. Call Andre.

options.label: “Your dad was probably lucky.”
options.reply: My dad is sitting in row four on Sunday, Maya.

options.label: “I'd rather not.”
options.reply: That's not a reason. That's a mood.

items.prompt: You have a load table and an estimate. How do you ask for help?
items.happening: The circuit was asked for more than it's built to carry.
items.lab_label: build the load plan you'll read to Andre.

options.label: Text: “breaker tripped, help”
options.result: Andre, driving: “Which breaker? What's on it?” He arrives without a plan.
options.consequence: The first hour of his visit goes to finding out what Maya already knew.
options.fail: A vague escalation makes the expert rediscover what you knew.

options.label: Call Andre with the table
options.result: Maya: what happened, when, what's on the circuit, her estimate, and what she hasn't touched.
options.consequence: Andre: “That's the most useful call I've had all week.” He comes with the right tools and a plan.

options.label: Wait until after Easter
options.result: Easter runs with half the lights and a dead keyboard amp.
options.consequence: Sofia's look is gone, and the unknown circuit is still unknown on Monday.

options.label: Ask Gus — he knows electrical
options.result: Gus: “I knew it forty years ago. It's not mine anymore, and it isn't yours.” Back to the choice.
options.consequence: Knowing something once isn't the same as being qualified now.
options.fail: Knowing something once isn't being qualified now.

items.alt: Maya on the phone to Andre, the electrician, with her load table in hand.

bubbles.text: Stage-left breaker tripped at 7:41 when twelve new fixtures went to full. My estimate: about 2,700 watts on it. Nothing's been opened or reset.

items.title: Ohm's law and Joule heating
items.body: Georg Ohm published the relation between voltage, current and resistance in 1827. In 1841 James Joule showed that current heats a wire in proportion to the current squared — the heat a breaker is built to notice before the wire does.

items.alt: Andre, on the phone at home.

bubbles.text: That's the most useful call I've had all week. Don't touch the panel. We'll be there at eight thirty. I'm bringing Malik.

items.alt: Andre, a journeyman electrician, and Malik, his apprentice in a hi-vis vest, arrive at the locked electrical room.

bubbles.text: Maya? Andre. This is Malik — my apprentice.
I've heard about your load table.

lines.text: Heard about your load table. Andre read it to me in the van. Twice.

items.alt: Andre unlocks the electrical room and works at the panel. Maya stays outside the taped line; Malik stands ready at the door with Andre's tester.
items.caption: Andre opens the panel. Everyone else stays on this side of the tape.

items.alt: Malik traces the stage outlets with a circuit tracer under Andre's direction. He sticks small labels on them: C3 on the stage-left wall, C5 on the stage-right wall.

bubbles.text: Stage left is all circuit 3. Stage right is circuit 5 — and it's carrying almost nothing.

items.title: Circuit 3: STAGE (TEMP) — 1998
items.body: Temporary for twenty-seven years. Someone added a fixture list in biro in 2009 and a question mark in 2016. The question mark is the most recent maintenance on record.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #6 · AVERY'S LENS  Make the safe path the easy path  When an action is dangerous, make the right next step obvious and fast.  A locked door with a phone number on it — call the electrician, here's what to say — is good design for a bad moment.

items.alt: Andre compares Maya's table with what he found.

bubbles.text: Your math matches mine. I plan a circuit like this to about 80 percent — that's my call, and codes vary.

items.caption: 80% of 2,400 W ≈ 1,920 W (example planning margin).

items.alt: Malik and Maya talk while Andre finishes at the panel.

bubbles.text: You did the math. I can do the math and open that door — when Andre says. That's the difference.
Know versus do.

items.caption: Malik: “Know versus allowed.”

items.prompt: Andre moves six fixtures to circuit 5 and resets the breaker. Sofia wants all twelve at full for the Easter opening. What do you tell her?
items.happening: The load is split across two circuits and the breaker is reset — by the electrician.
known: ◉ Outlets now labeled C3 and C5
unknown: What the full look actually draws

options.label: “It'll hold now”
options.consequence: Nobody has seen the full look at full power since the fix. Maya promised before she proved.

options.label: “Full-look test tonight”
options.result: All twelve fixtures at full, the band playing, thirty minutes — while Andre reads the current on both circuits.
options.consequence: Easter morning starts from a proof, not a hope.

options.label: “Keep them at 70 percent”
options.result: Sofia frowns: “Why seventy?” Maya can't say.
options.consequence: A guess dressed up as a rule.

options.label: “No new fixtures this year”
options.consequence: Safe and sad. Sofia stops telling the booth about her plans.

items.alt: 10:00 p.m. The full-look test: all twelve fixtures at full and the band playing. Andre's clamp meter reads about 15 amps on circuit 3 — an illustrative reading. Nothing trips for thirty minutes.
items.caption: Thirty minutes at full. No trip. (Readings illustrative; Andre measures.)

items.alt: Easter morning. The opening look blazes; the room is full. Nothing trips.
items.caption: Easter. Full room, full look. Nothing trips.

items.alt: In the booth, Lily checks the neighbors: the sound system's circuit is steady, the stream is clean, the keyboard and monitors on circuit 3 work.
items.caption: Adjacent checks: nothing next door broke.

items.alt: After the service, Sofia admits her blind spot.

bubbles.text: I planned the look. I didn't plan the power.
Next time, bring me the look and I'll bring Andre the table.

Andre shows Imani the panel's paper schedule taped inside the door.

bubbles.text: The stage is labeled now. The rest of this panel's labels are from 1998.
Put it on my list.

items.caption: DEBT-011 (draft): the building's panel schedule is out of date. Owner: Imani.

lines.text: You know how most calls go? “It's broken, come now.” You told me what, when, what's on it, and what you didn't touch.
Do that again and I'll pick up on the first ring.

items.alt: Ray reads the change-log entry and gives one principle.

bubbles.text: A breaker that trips is the building telling you the truth. Thank it — then call the person who's allowed to listen.

items.alt: Dolores comes to the booth holding an assistive listening receiver.

bubbles.text: I finally tried the little receiver, for the Easter reading. Nothing. Not a word.

items.caption: Next: *Nobody Could Hear the Reading.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Power is volts times amps; add the loads before you add the lights. A breaker that trips is doing its job. Know the arithmetic — and know whose door it is. The panel belongs to a licensed electrician, and a good escalation arrives with facts: what happened, when, what's on it, your estimate, and what you didn't touch.

REFLECTION (optional)  · Easter's light was the point of the morning; the circuit was only there to serve it. Stewardship includes knowing the limits of what you hold.  Boundary: none of this explains or proves the electrical fault.
